faqs.question: What is the Zeiss Stemi 355 used for?

faqs.question: What are the three configurations?
faqs.answer: Education, Labs, and Industry, each a ready-to-use set matched to its setting, with a different illumination system built in.

faqs.question: Does the specimen need to be prepared before viewing?

faqs.question: What illumination does each set include?
faqs.answer: Education has an LED spot for strong-shadow detail and a flat transmitted light base. Labs has a double-arm gooseneck for adjustable oblique lighting and a tiltable mirror base. Industry has a segmentable LED ringlight for shadow-free or oblique inspection.

faqs.question: Can images be captured and documented?

faqs.question: How many stand and tube options are available?
faqs.answer: Three stands and two tube options, which assemble into the configuration that fits the application.

faqs.question: Is Stemi 355 replacing another Zeiss model?

longForm.heroHook: No slide. No stain. No prep. Just the specimen, in 3D, exactly as it is.
longForm.heroLead: Some samples were never meant to sit under a coverslip. A beetle, a circuit board, a bullet, a root tip pulled straight from the soil, all need to be seen whole, in three dimensions, without any preparation getting in the way. Stemi 355 is built for exactly that. It comes as three ready-to-use sets, each configured for where it'll actually be used: Education, Labs, and Industry. Three stands and two tube options assemble into whichever combination the work calls for, and every version ships with integrated near-vertical LED illumination as standard. High-contrast, three-dimensional viewing comes standard across all three. Add a microscope camera to the phototube, and documentation happens on the spot, no separate setup required. What it skips: slide prep, staining, coverslips, anything the specimen shouldn't need in the first place. What it configures to: classroom, biology lab, or industrial inspection bench. What it succeeds: the Stemi 305, reaching end of sales shortly.

body: A compact stereo microscope for classrooms, biology labs, and industrial applications. Three ready-to-use sets, each matched to its setting.

Stemi 355 for Industry. Binocular tube, integrated near-vertical illumination, a segmentable LED ringlight for shadow-free or oblique segment illumination, and ESD-safe antistatic coating on the body and stand.

body: A stereo microscope built for a classroom doesn't need ESD protection, and one built for an electronics bench doesn't need to survive being carried between rooms every hour. Stemi 355 doesn't try to do all three jobs with one fixed setup, it ships as three distinct sets, each matched to the environment it'll actually live in.

Education is built to travel: easy to transport, easy to install, easy to use, with an LED spot for the strong-shadow detail that makes a specimen's texture obvious to a room full of students. Labs adds a double-arm gooseneck for variable oblique lighting, precisely the control a dissection actually needs as the angle of a cut changes. Industry swaps that gooseneck for a segmentable ringlight, shadow-free when the inspection needs even coverage, switchable to oblique segments when a defect needs raking light to show up, all on an ESD-safe body.

sections.title: Apochromatic Optics and the 8:1 Zoom
sections.description: What color accuracy and range actually mean at the eyepiece.
body: Standard stereo optics show color fringing at high magnification, a soft halo around edges that gets worse the further you zoom in. That's not a minor cosmetic issue when the work depends on distinguishing genuine material boundaries from optical artifacts. Apochromatic correction removes it, at every point across Stemi 508's zoom range.

The 8:1 zoom ratio means that correction holds from a 122 mm field of view down to the finest detail an interchangeable eyepiece and front optic combination can resolve, up to 250x. And because working distance stretches to 287 mm at the wide end, reaching that level of detail doesn't mean crowding tools, hands, or a soldering iron into a cramped gap under the objective.
